sections.heading: Random variables and distributions in Probability and Statistical Inference
paragraphs: Random variables and distributions is studied here as a specific part of Probability and Statistical Inference. Begin by defining the term precisely and identifying the problem it helps explain or solve. Keep the scope narrow: related ideas may interact with it, but they are not interchangeable.

Statistics separates describing observed data from drawing conclusions about a wider population. The sampling method, measurement process, missingness, and variability affect how much confidence a result deserves. A statistic is a sample summary; a parameter describes the population.

examples.title: Worked application: Confidence intervals
steps: A confidence interval is produced by a method with a stated long-run coverage rate under its assumptions. A 95% confidence procedure captures the fixed population parameter in 95% of repeated samples in the long run. After one interval is calculated, it is not strictly correct in the frequentist interpretation to say the fixed parameter has a 95% probability of lying inside that particular interval.
Identify the assumption or condition on which the explanation depends.
Apply the same principle to a changed case and state what would change in the result.
Write a conclusion that answers the question directly and notes one relevant limitation.
examples.note: Original Student Plug teaching example; not an official university solution or verified past examination question.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does a 95% confidence level describe?
options: Long-run coverage of the interval procedure under its assumptions
A 95% probability that every observation is correct
A guarantee that the sample has no bias
A 95% chance the null hypothesis is true
practiceQuestions.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run behaviour of the procedure, not certainty about a particular interval.

examples.title: Worked application: Hypothesis testing and errors
steps: A null hypothesis specifies a reference claim, while an alternative describes departures of interest. A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model and its assumptions, of obtaining data at least as incompatible with the null as the observed result. It is not the probability that the null is true and does not measure effect size.
Identify the assumption or condition on which the explanation depends.
Apply the same principle to a changed case and state what would change in the result.
Write a conclusion that answers the question directly and notes one relevant limitation.
examples.note: Original Student Plug teaching example; not an official university solution or verified past examination question.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean under the specified test model?
options: If the null and assumptions hold, results at least this extreme have probability 0.03
There is a 97% probability the research hypothesis is true
The effect is necessarily large
The data have a 3% chance of being real
practiceQuestions.explanation: The p-value is conditional on the null model; it is not a posterior probability of a hypothesis.
